story_written: I sit and I think is this really how things are going to end. I can't reach my partner because the phone keeps cutting out, and I hear no noise from their end. The house feels colder without their voice. I look for food but there isn't much left but a can of soup with a dented lid on the kitchen shelf. I grab a manual can opener from the drawer and pry it open slowly, I find some old stale bread tucked behind the magazine on the counter. I tear off a piece and take a small bite, then try calling again. The line goes cold nothing but silence. I set the phone down and pull a thin piece of bread on a plate, and I make the soup but try to ration it off carefully, knowing this might be all I have for tonight. The power flickers again, then goes out completely. I go into a small panic I can't reach my partner and I shuffle through drawers looking for the flashlight we keep by the stove, knock over a glass in my haste, and finally find it. It's working for now but I remember that I at least did make a small kit for emergencies that have more batteries, first aid kit, but I forgot to add food to it so now I sit down with the flashlight and can of soup, holding onto the hope that whatever happens next, I can get through at least. I wonder if I am going to have to go out and try to find my partner myself, even though I don't know if I'll make it, while I'm spiraling I find a few packs of seeds that I had always talked about planting one day but never got around to it. I wonder do seeds grow without regular water and if I could use some of the rainwater collected outside to keep them alive long. I also wonder if they expire before I even get a chance to plant them, or if they’ll still be good after all this waiting. I have to take that chance and bundle up before stepping outside into the dim light and just then I see my partner pull up in the driveway, their face tired but safe. I lower the flashlight and call out to them, my voice steady despite everything. They smile and they run to me giving me a hud. They brought what food they had because they knew I wouldn't have enough to last, some fresh fruit and a small loaf of bread from the corner store they managed to get before the power went out. We sat close together on the porch steps, peeling and eating quietly as the sky darkened and I wonder if everything is going to be okay.

Officials now say restoration will take longer, and your phone still shows no service.

It blooms near eye level and drifts toward the ceiling until the note ends. Then Drake’s voice on a higher syllable forms a small light blue ring above you. You lift your head and lean toward it as it spins past your face and fades.

A local TV alert finally comes through: attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; it’s knocked out more than GPS, because the satellites also carry timing signals banks and power utilities use, so card networks and parts of the grid are failing too.

By noon, your debit card is declined for gas and the ATM screen is blank. You count the few bills in your wallet at the register and put half the groceries back. In line, a radio mentions stalled traffic on Kellogg.

Days two through five, you drive by memory, conserving fuel, trying your spouse again from the car, from the porch, from a grocery parking lot. No signal holds. A cashier says banks are limiting withdrawals. One evening the lights cut out for an hour. By the fifth day, shelves are thin, officials say restoration will take longer, and you still have not reached them.

story_written: Bodies carpet the highway as I struggle through with other survivors. The military is shooting wildly at people who are taking advantage of the situation in order to grab supplies from abandoned vehicles and stores without permission. I drop to the side of the road, pressing my hands into the dirt to keep quiet as a fellow survivor crouches nearby, clutching a torn backpack filled with canned beans and a huge jar of water. The soldier's boots crunch past within feet of us, their rifles scanning left and right as they shout orders to move off the highway and find a safer route. I hold my breath and slowly shift my weight to keep from making noise, eyes watering as if I had taken a big whiff of smoke, while the soldier pauses briefly near a crushed car before stepping over it and moving on. I glance at the other survivor, their beanie sopping with sweat, and nod toward a narrow dirt path veering away from the carnage. At last, we stand and carefully follow the path through scrubby bushes and broken DVD players, stepping over tangled wires and shattered glass, the weight of the backpack pulling unevenly at my big ole gut, I keep my head low, listening for any sounds behind us while trying not to trip on the uneven bracken and peat bogs that slow our progress. After what feels like hours, the path opens onto an empty field where we pause to catch our breath and decide on the best way to divvy up our precious bean supply. I suggest we lay out the cans on a piece of cloth and split them into equal portions, making sure that we each get the good spicy ones and the plain ones, so neither of us ends up sad or feeling cheated. As we sit on the ground, I carefully count each can and arrange them in neat rows, making sure none are crushed or leaking. The other survivor unwraps a small, tattered cloth from their backpack, revealing a handful of dried jerky strips and a few hard candies. They offer to play cards.

story_written: If something I rely on daily stopped working, like my phone or internet connection, I would be lost. I use my phone and my internet daily, especially to communicate with my child and to get work done Today, when my messages stopped sending and the video calls froze mid-conversation, which freaked me out, because that never happened before I tried turning everything off and on, but nothing changed; when an alert went across the TV screen, I learned that a cyberattack had disabled satellite services nationwide. I quikly went outside to see if any of the the neighbors were outside or had a working phone, hoping to use theirs or at least neighbors were outside or if any cars were moving, hoping to find someone who might know what was going on. The street was unusually pretty quiet, but today, there were a few people standing by their porches, and I could tell they all had the same experience that I did Their faces were turned toward their phones or the sky, some shaking their heads, others speaking in low tones about calls that failed or radios that usually give great signal suddenly stopped playing news. One man was trying to call his office but gave up after several rings. A woman near the corner kept tapping her phone thinking that maybe it was just a glitch and then looked up at me, her brow wrinkled and confusion all over her face I walked over to her and asked if she had heard anything else on local channels, but she just shook her head and said they were all saying the same thing about cyber attacks, but then her TVs went out too I patted my pockets for cash, realizing I’d forgotten to grab any and started hurrying toward the corner store in case I was able to get to an ATM that was still working, but when I got there, the line to the ATM was packed, and everyone in front of the line was saying they couldn't withdraw any money because the machines had shut down along with everything else. I stood there, pushing my purse tighter against me, worried, confused and trying not to panic I looked around for a payphone or anyone willing to lend me their phone, and I saw a young child playing on a porch swing nearby, her mother sitting beside her with a phone in hand—but the phone in her hand was starting to glitch just like everyone elses phone I swallowed hard and stepped closer, asking if I could try calling my child to at least make sure they were safe The woman handed me the phone hesitantly, her eyes never leaving the screen as it flickered and froze

I shifted my grip slightly, and showed up the book that he wrote, letting the light catch the title clearly. Uketsu’s eyes followed my hand, and he was interested in which part of the story I was reading. He nodded thoughtfully and asked if that chapter had changed how I saw the characters. I blinked again, "How can you imagine such a complex story but everything is closely related to each other?" I said, my voice barely above a whisper. Uketsu smiled faintly and leaned in a bit closer, lowering his voice to match the quiet of the bookstore. I swallowed and nodded slowly, then reached into my bag to pull out a notebook filled with my own notes and sketches about the story. It was such a rare moment that I unconsciously took a step back to clear the small space between my favourite authorise and me. My hand trembled slightly as I closed the notebook, careful not to make a sound. I told him that I had no cure but then when I read to the end, everything was actually put in front of me and I was so amazed of his brillant ability to piece the plot so perfectly that it felt like discovering a hidden map. Uketsu nodded and glanced at my notebook again, asked, "Do you write often? ?" I nodded, my fingers tightening around the book as a soft murmur of voices and footsteps drifted in. "Would you like to read my story?" I blinked once more, then slowly opened my notebook for him to see the pages filled with my handwriting and drawings. Uketsu took the notebook carefully with both hands, his eyes scanning the pages quickly but with clear interest. He turned a few pages, his finger tracing some lines as he asked about the inspirations behind. We chatted about an hour until the bookstore has to close. He handed the notebook back to me gently and said, "Keep writing. You have a strong voice." I closed the notebook, folding the edges slightly to protect it, and silently promised myself I would write more often, just like he did.

I asked him how he was dealing with the lack of technology, and he responded, "It's tough," he said, rubbing the back of his neck. "We’re relying on radios that only operate on minimal frequencies." I asked him what he thought happened, and he said, "It's not a regular outage or something like that. They found out the ground control systems for satellites got hacked." I nodded and wearily approached the checkout line.

The bass line produces heavy orange bars that slide low beside the machine, one for each note, then fade as each note ends. A brighter guitar chord releases a yellow slab at chest height. It blooms wider because it is louder, then thins away. Steve Perry’s first high vocal note lets out a pale yellow ribbon near the ceiling. It hangs for the length of the note, then dissolves. You lean forward to follow it. Another snare hit throws a sharp orange tile past your knee, and you pull back.

story_written: I was in the kitchen that day, the day when sound became more real and colors began to appear before me as I listened to my music. It had been a fairly ordinary day up until then until the high piano notes in the chorus kicked in and I began to sing as I was drying dishes. The high piano notes released small pale yellow triangles that floated near my head and I reached up slowly but stopped just short as one spun past my ear, its sharp edges bristling past me. The music continued, but I spotted the drum beats, sending heavy dark red spheres skimming just above my feet across the floor tiles. I shifted my weight back from the base notes, trying to keep from screaming. I stepped carefully to the side, watching as a magenta rectangle glided in with the steady bass guitar line, hanging low near the floor before it disappeared. I stopped the music to see what would happen and the kitchen grew silent, and the brightly colored shapes slowly faded away like mist. I took a deep breath and pressed play again as Beyonce launched into the chorus and once again the small pale yellow triangles appeared near my head. I moved the dish towel to one hand, and with my free hand, I reached out cautiously toward a cluster of pale yellow triangles swirling just above the countertop light. As I reached for them, they shifted and moved around me in a slow circle, the sharp points catching the kitchen light and casting tiny flickers on the cabinets. I stayed still, watching them, holding my breath. Beyonce's voice hung in the air, golden and sweet just above the doorway, a large soft ribbon that gently swayed back and forth. Amazed, I lowered my hand and took a step back, eyes fixed on the golden ribbon as it drifted slowly toward the ceiling fan, twisting softly in the warm kitchen air while the next piano chord sent a cluster of orange squares bouncing off the refrigerator door.

A push alert finally comes through: attackers breached a satellite ground station through a VPN vulnerability and deployed malware that wiped connected systems; GPS is down, and the satellite timing signals that banks and power grids use are failing too. You count the cash in your wallet and put back half your groceries. You call your spouse twice to make sure they’re safe; one call drops, the next never connects. On day three, you use a paper map from the glove box, pay cash for canned food, and hear a radio mention stalled traffic and banks limiting withdrawals. By day five, shelves are thin, the lights cut out for an hour at a time, and you still cannot reach your spouse.

story_written: I didn't realize at first that Mo Salah, Liverpool FC and Egyptian legend, was standing right behind me, asking me if I wanted to ride a bike with him around the lake. I stuttered at first, but then answered nervously, "Yeah, I've ridden it a couple of times. Beautiful scenery all around." He smiled and asked if I wanted to join him on the ride with him and his family. I laughed and shook my head, "That seems like a personal trip you should take yourself. I wouldn't feel right joining you." Mo Salah checked his watch and inched closer to the bikes. "I'll pay for you. Just a quick lap is all." I had no excuse to say no, so I decided to join him on the trip. The fresh breeze washed our faces as we pedaled along the gravelly path, bumping up and down. "I can't believe I'm biking with Mo Salah. THE Mo Salah!" I exclaimed. He laughed it off. "Most Celtics fans are Liverpool fans as well. Have you ever been to a game?" I shook my head with an ounce of sadness. "I actually went to a game back in January," I said, "but you were playing AFCON. I never got to see you play." Mo Salah smiled. "Send me your number, my friend. I'll get you tickets for Turkiye to watch Trabonzoor play. But first, let's finish this ride."

The man behind me tapped his phone, attempting to be a gentleman and pay for me, assuming I was just broke and trying to spare me some embarassment. His phone produced the same non-reaction. We made eye contact and he shook his head slowly, tiled his head puzzled. and muttered, "Not working." I glanced at the ATM in the lobby, it's screen dark with red letters- ERROR. I glanced at the man and said "I believe we have entered unprecedented territory".  The kind workers behind the counter said "it's on the house, don't worry about it.... you guys will be our last orders of the day" I nodded, pocketing the few bills I had left. Outside, cars sat idle, their computer systems unresponsive, and I noticed a few drivers stepping out, looking around in confusion. Luckily my car started right up, sometimes not being about to afford the newest models has its advantages. I was never one to depend on GPS either, so I was able to find my way back to my side of town with relative ease, navigating carefully around stalled cars. I knew looting would begin soon, if what i thought was going on was going on. To be honest, i had NO IDEA what was going on.... But i knew i needed to make sure my parents were safe, and I pulled over to the side of the road, trying to make a list of supplies we'd all need, and who i needed to check on. Also, I tried to think of major corporations like Wal-Mart i wouldn't feel bad about pilaging , if it came down to it. Nobody in my circle was going to die of deyhydration if I could help it, and the afternoon sun was already pressing down hard so I stopped at a small corner store that was open, paying for cases of bottled water with my last few bills- i had more cash at home, and i'd also grab a ski mask, just incase... Time to find my family,  i thought. And make sure my fiance isn't going crazy, i imagined him at his work desk, frustrated and unable to log in, the office computers frozen like everything else. I tried calling his number again, holding the line, nothing. not even straight to voicemail. I decided i'd go by his office first, as at least my parents were probably together. I didn't want him to be alone and freaking out, and his mind would be better occupied if I was there with him. The office building loomed ahead, its parking lot nearly empty except for his car, which was a newer model. He was sitting in it freaking out. fighting a losing battle with the key. "jump in" i said as i rolled down the window to say something as I reached over to help him open it, and the door finally clicked open. He sighed, rubbing his forehead before sliding over to the passenger seat. We sat there for a moment. "I gotta find my parents now, we'll get your car later. grab anything you might need, also if there's any food or drink in the office fridge, let's grab it. it's gonna get bad out here....."

I reminded myself they were both probably at work and nothing nefarious was likely going on with their house. I walked to the end of their driveway and looked down both sides of the street noticing no one was around and every house looked dark and quiet. It gave me the creeps and I hotfooted it back to the safety of my home. I locked and bolted the door behind me as soon as I walked in and then checked the backdoor and windows. I told myself there was no reason to be so paranoid but the overwhelming sense of dread was very real.

This would freak me out as I live alone and rely on my phone to check on my family and vice versa. I would probably try to call each of my family members multiple times through phone, text, and maybe even trying my computer. I would also start to mildly freak out because the next thing I would do would be to go to the internet or social media to see if this was happening to anyone else. I would probably try turning on and off my Wifi several times and I may even leave my apartment to go outside to see if I got service out there. If I was at work it would be a better scenario as I would not be able to get my work done as I rely on computer but I would have my coworkers to be there for support and assistance. If a significant amount of time had passed of me being home with no internet connection I would at some point get in my car and drive to my parent's house to be with them.

The ATM by the door shows an error screen. On your phone, an alert says attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; GPS is down, and the same satellites provide timing for banks and parts of the power grid, so payment networks and utilities are failing too. You count the cash in your wallet and put back the extra food. You call your close friend twice to make sure he’s safe; one call drops, the next never connects. By day three, you’re using side streets from memory, stretching bills, hearing a radio mention stalled traffic and seeing a bank notice about withdrawal limits. On day five, after another failed call and a short power cut, the store shelves are thinner and the official update says restoration will take longer.

Your fingers go to the brim. Then away. Then back again.

He gives the cap a small nod. “I used to watch people by their hats. They tell you things.”

You open your mouth, stop, and glance at the books in his hand before trying again.

He asks if you always wear that cap on your route. You answer, and he listens closely. Then he asks what you read, what kind of stories stay with you, and what kind never do.

story_written: When I went to go start on my volunteer role for a local track promoter I had noticed that my laptop wasn't connecting to the internet or any services, I usually play music while I work so this was off putting for me. But I put my laptop aside and walked over to the small radio sitting on the counter. I turned it on just for it to not work, I flipped the switch, and nothing came out except static; the red light did not come on either. I checked if it was plugged in and saw that the power cord was loose. I pushed it firmly into the outlet, and still just pure radio silence. So I had to go the old fashion route of pulling out my CD player and playing some rock music from a compilation disc I found in my drawer. I wiped off the dust from the CD before sliding it into the player. The mechanical whir of the CD player brought back so many memories of riding around with friends and blasting this exact album on long summer nights. I tapped my fingers on the counter to the beat and finally got to work. Although the services were out I still enjoyed my time writing for this social media post, and I just felt purely nostalgic as I typed out the words slowly, glancing up now and then at the empty room around me. The quiet hum from the CD player filled the room steadily while I organized flyers and schedules on the counter. Every so often, and by the time I knew it I was done and had wrote over 100 posts I leaned back in my chair, stretched my arms above my head, and just relaxed on my couch from a hard days work.

The hour-long drive home from college for the weekend was still one I was adjusting to, and my phone's GPS that had previously easily shown me the way home had frozen on the screen, not moving it all. After a moment, the entire screen went dark. I pulled over to the side of the road and turned my phone off and on again, but when it powered back, the screen refused to unlock at all. I sighed to myself. "Of course now is the time to have phone troubles," I mutter, trying not to panic as I looked around for any familiar landmarks. The fields on either side of the road stretched out flat and empty. It was official, I was completely and utterly lost. I knew there was not much else to do but follow on the road I'd been taking.

A push alert says attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; GPS is down, and the timing signals banks and power utilities use are failing too. You call to check if your child is safe, but the call drops, then won’t connect. Over the next four days, you stretch the cash in your wallet, use side streets you can remember, and keep trying that number. A cashier mentions rolling outages. A radio near a checkout counter says banks are limiting withdrawals. By day five, one grocery shelf is bare, your phone still shows no route, and you still have not reached your child.

journal_shown_to_user: You are at a pharmacy in Saint Petersburg, tapping your card for toothpaste and bottled water when the reader freezes, then flashes error. The cashier tries again, then shrugs and points to a handwritten sign: cash only. Your bank app will not load, and the ATM by the door is dark. In the parking lot, a news alert says attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; the satellites also carry timing signals banks and power grids use, so payments and utilities are failing too. You call your close friend twice to check that you both have food and water, but the calls drop. By day three, you are counting small bills, driving by memory, hearing a radio mention stalled traffic and seeing a bank notice about withdrawal limits. On day five, shelves are thinner, the power blinks off again, and your friend still does not answer.

story_written: My partner and I stay at home, wondering when things will be back to normal. Neither of us can work so we spend the day sorting through old papers and cleaning cupboards. The tasks are mundane, but they keep us sane. We try to figure out which food supplies we have left that don’t require refrigeration, and how to make meals out of what we've got until the grocery stores are open again. We take inventory of canned goods, dried pasta, and bags of rice, noting expiration dates and making a rough plan for meals. We feel thankful that we've stock piled a good amount of food and set aside some drinking water in case the tap water supply becomes unreliable. After dinner, we light candles to see by since the power is still out. We talk the evening away, and feel closer. Almost happy that the TV is still out since we spent too much time staring at it. We sit side by side on the couch, each holding a candle, and look into each other eyes, grateful to have each other. This event was so unexpected, but having a routine to follow and each other made the scary circumstances so much less scary. Our cat is curled up on the rug, completely unaware that anything is amiss. Luckily we had plenty of his food so I filled his bowl and placed it near the back door where he usually likes to eat and then I checked that the water dish was full. He purred and had his dinner, then settled down beside us, his steady breathing filling the quiet room as we planned what to do tomorrow without knowing when anything would change.

I shifted my position in my chair, not necessarily fearful but cautious, as a deep bass note rolled out and produced a large, heavy brown cube that settled near my desk I reached out my hand slowly, stopping just short of touching the cube, watching it pulse slightly in time with the beat before a quick beat change, a loud, chirp synth stab released a thin pale gray spike that shot upward, then, evolved into a gradient I leaned forward slightly, eyes fixed on the gradient spike as it stretched toward the ceiling. I'm not on drugs and I'm sitting right here in my bedroom, holding onto the arms of this chair. The music keeps playing and every sound makes a shape, do I need to see a doctor or someone who understands this? The bass drops again, sending a wide dark brown rectangle sliding slowly across the floor near my feet, I'm not in pain, I'm not fearful, but I shift my weight slightly to the side so I don't accidentally kick it. The snare hits, this can't be real right surely I must be mistaking my tired mind for something strange. The next drum hit sends a sharp charcoal zigzag darting over me, it's time to see a specialist who can help me understand what's happening. I stand up slowly, still watching the shapes form, I'm in no shape to be moving quickly around the room. A low, steady bass thump creates a series of dark olive cylinders thud, maybe its time to turn off the music and sit quietly to see if the shapes disappear. I step back carefully, avoiding the cylinders as they roll toward the dresser. The muted green notes disappear, but other noises, even non musical notes —like the clicking of the keyboard from my laptop—send out faint shapes too. A small, dark gray cube, once more, almost like frequencies have become visible A small, dark gray cube, once more, emerges as I WebMD myself into a fog of medical articles and forum posts, leaning against the desk, let's just get an Uber and head to the clinic. The music plays on, and with each sound a new shape forms—this time a thin black line tracing, not really, I turned it off.

The air smells like sunscreen, hot pavement, and fried food from the place next door. You stop near the door and look down, then back up, then shift your weight and tighten your grip on the pack.

Britney Spears stands a few feet away in a baseball cap and loose tank top. She gives a small nod toward the cigarettes and says she quit years ago but still notices the pack design every time. You let out a short laugh, glance away, and start to answer. She stays right there and asks what you were about to buy. Then she asks if you come here a lot, and the talk keeps going.

journal_shown_to_user: You stop at a gas station in an Albany suburb on your way back from a coffee shop, tap your card, and the screen freezes. Inside, the clerk tries twice, then points to the ATM, already showing an error screen. Your phone finally loads an alert: attackers breached a satellite ground station through a VPN vulnerability and used malware to wipe connected systems; GPS is down, and the satellites’ timing signals that banks and power grids use are failing too. You count the cash in your wallet and buy only gas and a sandwich. In the parking lot, you call your mom about her health problems; the call drops, then won’t reconnect. Over the next four days, you stretch bills, follow handwritten directions, and keep trying her number. A radio mentions stalled traffic. A checkout line leaves carts behind. On day five, the power blinks out again, and her phone still does not ring.

journal_shown_to_user: You’re in your driveway in suburban Massachusetts, refreshing a radar page and texting your aunt before heading in, when both the weather site and your messages freeze. Your phone shows bars, then none. A push alert finally loads: attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; GPS is down, and the same satellites provide timing for banks and parts of the power grid, so payment networks and utilities are failing too. At the gas station, your card is declined twice, and the ATM screen is black; you count the few bills in your wallet and leave with less than half a tank. Calls to your father drop before ringing. Over a battery radio: stalled traffic, banks limiting withdrawals. By day four, you’re using printed roads, buying only what cash covers, trying his number morning and night, and the store near you has bare shelves and dim lights while officials say service will take longer.

story_written: I need to get to the child care location to pick up my son, but the phones are not working. I check the time on my watch, grab my keys from the counter, and start walking quickly toward the daycare center since I can't call them to make sure everything is okay. The smoke is thickening as I move down the street, and my throat feels irritated. I try to stay close to the ground where the air seems clearer, pulling my shirt up over my nose as I focus on how many steps it takes to get from one block to the next, counting each footfall against the rising noise of distant fire engines, the cracking of burning wood, and voices calling out directions. My eyes water and they are stinging from the smoke, so I blink rapidly and pause at a corner to find a tissue. I have to keep moving because my son needs me, so I put the tissue in my pocket, and tighten my grip on the keys in my hand. I look around for any other parents who might be heading toward the daycare too, hoping to join up and help each other navigate through the smoke and possible roadblocks. I decide not to try entering and instead look around for another way to reach Jason or someone else. I am so close to the daycare now that I can see its fenced yard through the smoke, but a fire engine blocks the street just past it, and a firefighter asks me what I need and points toward a side alley where emergency personnel are guiding parents to a temporary pickup spot. I see Jason and all is well.

“Still wearing that?” Tom Brady taps the brim of your Patriots hat before you even turn around.

It is a regular Saturday afternoon at the coffee shop near downtown Greenville where you often stop after a walk. The grinder is running. Ice knocks against plastic cups behind the counter. You spin around so fast your chair scrapes the floor, then you stand up right away and nearly leave your drink behind.

Tom Brady gives a quick smile and points at the hat again. “That’s old school. Where’d you get it?”

You grab the brim and answer too fast, then laugh and pull the chair out with your foot. He asks if he can sit for a minute. You nod at once.

He sits across from you and asks if you come here every weekend. You ask what brought him through Greenville. He answers in an easy, calm way, then asks what kind of work you do.

I laugh softly and say, "Yeah, you never know when your going to be stranded on a desert island and might need to power up your phone for help or entertainment." I shift my weight and glance toward the booth again, noticing the bright colors. "I love that sculpture you picked out." Christopher Walken gives a small smile and replies, "It's the colors. "This is a perfect spot to sit and talk," I say, settling down in the little nook next to the wooden bench. Christopher sets his cup carefully on the ground and leans back, folding his hands in his lap. "I cannot wait to tell you the story." Christopher reached into his jacket pocket, producing a smaller charger with a grin, saying he needs to walk around with a backup too, since he never knows when inspiration will strike and the phone will start buzzing nonstop. I matched his grin and this starts the greatest night of my life!

story_written: I can't believe this is really happening. I  walked outside to check the traffic lights at the main intersection near my house. The street was quiet. Where is everyone, I wondered as I saw a car stopped halfway through the crosswalk, its hazard lights blinking. A man stood beside it, with his face in his hands and a small boy clung to his leg, looking around nervously. I stepped closer. Are you okay, I asked as the man looked up and wiped his face with the back of his hand. He nodded slowly but didn't say anything. so I gestured toward the darkened traffic light and asked if he needed help crossing. He glanced down at the boy, then back at me and nodded again. I took the boy’s small hand and carefully guided them both across the street, stepping around scattered debris. The boy's hand feels good in mine. It's reassuring to feel human contact when everything else seems to have stopped working. After I helped them across, I watched them  walk slowly down the sidewalk, their footsteps uneven on the cracked pavement. The man kept looking over his shoulder as if checking for something or looking for someone and the boy held tightly onto his coat, never letting go as they disappeared around the corner. I stood there for a few minutes after they had gone, listening to the quiet hum of the neighborhood.

story_written: While listening to my favorite song, I watched as a rainbow of colors suddenly emerged around me. At first, I was confused but then I noticed that the shapes matched each sound exactly. When the drum hit, I saw a row of black circles appear in front of me, each one popping into existence. Later, when the bass rhythm was strong, I stepped back as a series of large dark clouds of grey surrounded me. I tried turning on another song to see if the colors would go away, but they only got more vivid. This time, I stood still and watched as a sharp, black rectangle shot out from the desk with each snare hit. I wondered if I could touch the colors, and I reached out slowly with my hand, stopping just before a black circle popped near my fingertips. It disappeared the moment I got close. I tried again, and a small pale oval floated up near the ceiling. Still, I could not reach the shapes without making them vanish, so I decided to step back to the corner of the room and observe how each sound created a new shape. Would there be consistency to the sounds and their corresponding shapes and colors? I watched a bright white ribbon rise above the lamp as Sara's voice held a note, its edges soft. This shapes and colors continued to match the tone of the music, and I started to predict what would come next. For example, a quick drum roll sent a sharp row of small black triangles darting across the wall each time the chorus began. I wondered if these shapes would ever go away, and I moved closer to the laptop and paused the song. Suddenly, the shapes vanished, and the room around me returned to its plain black, white, and grey colors. I folded the cloth quietly while glancing at the room returned to its usual monochrome tones. I folded the cloth again, noticing how quiet it felt without the sounds and the absence of shapes made the space look empty. I put the cloth down on the desk, then sat in my chair and opened a journal to write down my feelings. Would the shapes ever re turn if I played the song again? I pressed play and watched as a dull grey block formed near the floor with the first low piano note. I leaned forward slightly, keeping my eyes fixed on the block as it held its shape softly.

A soft green circle glided to the ceiling, glowing gently as Morgan’s sustained vocal note held steady. This happened as the guitar strum released a series of small, sharp purple circles that popped quickly in rhythm with the beat I shifted my grip on the elliptical bars and watched each circle appear briefly near the blue ribbons, indigo slabs, and green ovals. My legs kept moving steadily while I followed the shapes with my eyes. A bass note made a pale green cube rise slowly from the floor near my left foot. I have leaned forward slightly, eyes fixed on the pale green cube as it ascended on the steady beat, noticing how its edges softened as the note sustained. Another sharp purple circle popped near it in time with the guitar strum and I adjusted my pace to match the rhythm, feeling the steady movement of my legs. I shifted my weight to keep balance as the pale green cube floated up, then glanced sideways at the bright blue ribbon twisting lightly above the console. A quick drum hit sent a small purple square snapping out from the right side and it struck the side of the elliptical bar with a clean edge before disappearing instantly. I tightened my grip for a second and stepped a little faster, matching the drum’s quick pulse as another purple circle popped near the console, sharply defined and vanishing immediately. A deep indigo block formed near my left foot, large and heavy-looking. It slid forward slowly with the bass line’s low note, then dissolved as the music shifted to the next measure. I eased my pace, watching a pale blue oval float up near the ceiling with a higher vocal note. I leaned back slightly, keeping my hands steady on the bars as a series of small green spheres appeared on the left side, each one pulsing in time with the beat and rising slowly toward the ceiling. A sharp purple triangle popped sharply near my hand I adjusted my grip quickly, watching it vanish as the next drum hit sent a similar shape snapping from the console. This continued through the song, each new sound creating a distinct shape that I followed closely while my feet moved in time. I slowed my movements as the final vocal note released a faint pale green oval that drifted slowly upward, its edges glowing softly and hovered just below the ceiling. I kept my hands steady on the bars and watched it fade gradually, matching the beat with a final slow pedal stroke. A soft blue wave undulated gently near the top of the console as the song shifted to a sustained guitar note. I straightened my posture and focused on the soft blue wave, noticing how it pulsed with each sustained guitar note, its edges smoothing and expanding slowly as my legs continued their steady rhythm on the elliptical. I moved my hands slightly to follow the wave's motion, careful not to lose my grip on the bars, and adjusted my breathing to stay steady while the blue wave expanded and contracted in time with the guitar's beat. I kept my eyes on the soft blue wave as it grew brighter and larger,

The first bass line produces a large deep blue block near the floor beside the machine. It slides forward with the beat and dissolves at once. A drum hit sends a sharp purple square out from the console. It snaps against the side rail and vanishes. The next drum hit sends another square in the same rhythm. Morgan Wallen’s first vocal note releases a small pale green oval higher up, just under the ceiling. It blooms while he holds the note, then fades. A higher vocal turn releases a thinner, brighter blue ribbon above it. You lean toward it. Another loud bass note produces a bigger dark indigo slab by your shoes. You pull your foot back as it spreads, then disappears.

The clerk tries again, then points to the ATM by the door: out of service. Your phone finally loads a state alert saying attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; GPS is down, and the satellites’ timing signals that banks and power grids use are down too, so card networks and utilities are failing. You have a few dollars in your wallet. You call your husband to check that he’s okay; the call drops twice, then won’t connect. By day three, you’re counting bills at checkout, driving side streets from memory, hearing a radio mention stalled traffic and seeing a bank notice about withdrawal limits. On day five, after another failed call and a dark grocery aisle, officials say restoration will take longer.

A phone alert says attackers got into a satellite ground station through a VPN flaw and used malware to wipe connected systems; GPS is down, and the same satellites provide timing that banks and parts of the power grid need, so payments and utilities are failing too. You count the bills in your wallet twice. You call your parent to figure out where to meet, but the call drops, then won’t connect.

A bank window sign says withdrawals are limited. On day four, the lights cut out for an hour at the grocery store, and half the shelves are bare. You try your parent again each morning and each evening, and officials now say service will take longer than first expected.

Then I look at the weather and traffic before I head out to work. but today the weather app won't load, and when I open the traffic section, it just stays blank. I try my laptop to see if it connects to the internet, but the browser won’t connect to any website. I shut the laptop and pick up my phone to try again but the screen stays frozen on the home page. I press the power button a few times, but nothing ha ppens. I set the phone down and walk to the kitchen, hoping a cup of coffee will help me think through what’s going on. I fill the coffee maker and wait as it brews, glancing out the window at the empty street beyond my yard. Everything seems to be at a standstill and I realize there is no sound of cars passing by or neighbors. I try to relax with my coffee but at the kitchen radio, a voice breaks through with a burst of static before settling into an announcement about hackers.  Fear takes over and I set the mug down too hard, the ceramic thudding loudly on the counter. I lean forward to listen to the news broadcast and hear that the attackers breached a satellite ground station through a VPN vulnerability, deploying malware that wiped connected systems. I wake up my husband to let him know what is going on and we sit in the dark living room, listening quietly as the radio explains more about how this isn’t just our internet outage but a nationwide disruption affecting GPS, banking systems, and utilities. We decide to check with neighbors and drive to family homes nearby, making sure their phones still have some signal and that they have water or food supplies. The roads are chaotic as others have no clue what to do.

story_written: I stood at the sink, my mouth still half-open from where I'd been getting ready to sing along with the song, and watched as the long golden curve of the first line of the song started to fade away. The light from the kitchen window streamed down onto the sink, and Buffett's voice blended perfectly with the rays of sunlight through the blinds. The arc of his voice lifted and shimmered in the air like the mid-afternoon sun, and I wondered if it was just my mind playing tricks on me or, if I just reached out, I'd be able to touch the shape of my favorite song. I let the dishcloth fall from my fingers, landing in the sink along with the low, steady sounds of the bass line bubbling into blue-golden streams along the lines of the metal sink. My shoulders swayed unconsciously with the music, and my eyes followed the bright orange pulse of the steel drum as it bounced lightly off the ceiling, each beat sending a small warm circle across the shadows on the ceiling. I worked up the nerve to reach out, my fingers steady in the air and my body moving with the rhythm of the music, and I stopped just short of touching it. The golden line of the melody pulsed in the air at eye level, stretching wider as the next note began. I reached out to touch...and the music faded away, leaving me to turn, looking around my kitchen, which looked much the same as always.
